stem: What does the decimal for {{4|11}} look like?

choices.why: Right! 4 ÷ 11 = 0.3636…, and the 36 keeps repeating.
You stopped dividing too soon. Keep going: the 36 comes back again and again.
You copied the digits of the fraction. Divide 4 ÷ 11 instead.
2.75 is 11 ÷ 4. The fraction bar means 4 ÷ 11 (top ÷ bottom).

hint: Divide the top by the bottom: 4 ÷ 11. Does it stop, or does a block come back?
explain: The remainders repeat, so the block 36 repeats forever.
A repeating decimal is a rational number.

stem: Which choice gives a correct definition of an irrational number AND a correct example?

choices.t: It can't be written as a fraction of integers. Example: √{2}
choices.why: Right! √{2} = 1.41421… never ends and never repeats.

choices.t: It can't be written as a fraction of integers. Example: √{9}
choices.why: The definition is right, but √{9} = 3 = {{3|1}}, so √{9} is rational.

choices.t: It is a number less than zero. Example: −5
choices.why: Negative numbers can be rational. −5 = {{−5|1}}.

choices.t: It is a decimal that repeats. Example: 0.333…
choices.why: A repeating decimal is rational. 0.333… = {{1|3}}.

hint: Rational numbers can be written as a fraction of two integers. Irrational numbers can't.
explain: Rational: can be written as {{a|b}} with integers a and b (b ≠ 0). Its decimal stops or repeats.
Irrational: can't be written that way. Its decimal never ends and never repeats.
√{2} = 1.41421356… never ends or repeats, so it is irrational.

stem: Each decimal keeps the pattern shown. Which number is irrational?

choices.why: Right! The block keeps growing, so no block repeats and it never ends.
The block 10 repeats forever. A repeating decimal is rational.
This decimal stops (terminates). A terminating decimal is rational.
This decimal stops. Negative decimals that stop are still rational.

hint: Rational decimals stop or repeat the SAME block forever.
explain: 0.1010010001… has 1 zero, then 2, then 3, … The block keeps changing.
It never ends and never repeats, so it is irrational.

stem: Which list names every set that the number 0 belongs to?

choices.why: Right! 0 is whole, an integer, and rational (0 = {{0|1}}).
Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3, … We don't start counting at 0.
0 IS a whole number. The whole numbers are 0, 1, 2, 3, …
0 is also rational, because 0 = {{0|1}}, a fraction of integers.

hint: Natural numbers start at 1. Whole numbers start at 0.
explain: 0 = {{0|1}}, so 0 is rational. It is not irrational.

stem: Jayla's calculator shows 0.185185185… (the block 185 repeats). Write this number as a fraction in simplest form.

choices.why: Right! {{185|999}} simplifies to {{5|27}}.
{{37|200}} = 0.185, which stops. The decimal repeats, so use 9s, not 1000.
The block has 3 digits, so use 999, not 99. ({{185|99}} is more than 1!)
You used only 18 as the block. The repeating block is 185 (3 digits).

hint: The repeating block has 3 digits, so put it over 999.
explain: The repeating block is 185, which has 3 digits.
Check: 5 ÷ 27 = 0.185185… ✓ It's a fraction of integers, so it is rational.

stem: Marcus says 0.12112111211112… is rational "because it has a pattern." (Each time, one more 1 comes before the next 2.) Which answer is correct?

choices.t: No. It never ends and no block repeats, so it is irrational.
choices.why: Right! The runs of 1s keep getting longer, so no fixed block repeats.

choices.t: Yes. It has a pattern, so it must be rational.
choices.why: A pattern is not the same as repeating. Rational decimals repeat the SAME block.

choices.t: Yes. It only uses 1s and 2s, so the digits repeat.
choices.why: Using the same digits is not repeating. The block 12, 112, 1112… keeps changing.

choices.t: No. It is less than 1, so it must be irrational.
choices.why: Being less than 1 does not matter. 0.5 is less than 1 and is rational.

hint: Does the SAME block of digits repeat forever, or does it keep changing?
explain: Rational decimals stop, or repeat the SAME block forever.
Here the blocks are 12, 112, 1112, 11112, … They keep getting longer.
So no fixed block repeats, and the decimal never ends.
Marcus is wrong: the number is irrational.

stem: Which number is sorted correctly, with a correct reason?

choices.why: Right! 18 ÷ 3 = 6, a counting number, so it is in all four sets.

choices.t: −√{25}: irrational, because it has a square root sign
choices.why: 25 is a perfect square: −√{25} = −5. So it is an integer and rational.

choices.t: 4.222…: irrational, because the decimal never ends
choices.why: The 2 repeats forever. A repeating decimal is rational (but not an integer).

choices.t: 0: natural, whole, integer, rational, because 0 is counting
choices.why: We count starting at 1, so 0 is not natural. It is whole, integer, rational.

hint: Simplify each number first. Then check: does it stop, repeat, or neither?

visual.alt: A Real Numbers box holds a Rational box and a separate Irrational box. Inside Rational are nested boxes: Integers, then Whole, then Natural.

choices.t: A number either can be a fraction of integers or can't. It is never both.
choices.why: Right! The two sets don't overlap, and together they make all real numbers.

choices.t: Irrational numbers are bigger than rational numbers, so they get their own box.
choices.why: Size does not matter. √{2} ≈ 1.4 is irrational, and 100 is rational.

choices.t: Irrational numbers are all negative, so they go on the other side.
choices.why: Irrational numbers can be positive, like π, or negative, like −√{2}.

choices.t: Irrational numbers are not real numbers, so they are kept apart.
choices.why: The Irrational box is inside the Real box. Irrational numbers ARE real.

hint: Can one number be a fraction of integers and also NOT be one?
explain: Each box inside another means "every one of these is also one of those." Every natural number is whole, every whole number is an integer, and every integer is rational.
Rational means it CAN be written as a fraction of integers.
Irrational means it CAN'T. No number can be both.
So the two boxes don't overlap. Together they fill the Real Numbers box.

stem: Devon says, "{{2π|5}} is rational because it is written as a fraction." Which argument is correct?

choices.t: Devon is wrong. 2π is irrational, so {{2π|5}} is irrational too.
choices.why: Right! The top must be an integer, but 2π is irrational, and dividing by 5 keeps it irrational.

choices.t: Devon is right. Any number written as a fraction is rational.
choices.why: The top and bottom must both be integers. Here the top, 2π, is not.

choices.t: Devon is wrong. {{2π|5}} ≈ 1.26, and decimals are never rational.
choices.why: Many decimals are rational, like 0.4 = {{2|5}}. The real reason is π.

choices.t: Devon is right. π ≈ 3.14, so {{2π|5}} = {{6.28|5}}, a fraction.
choices.why: 3.14 is only an estimate of π. The exact value of 2π is not an integer.

hint: Rational means a fraction of two INTEGERS. Is 2π an integer?
explain: Rational: can be written as {{a|b}} where a and b are integers.
In {{2π|5}}, the top is 2π. π is irrational, so 2π is not an integer.
Dividing an irrational number by 5 keeps it irrational: {{2π|5}} = 1.2566…, never ending or repeating.

stem: Kai starts with a positive number and squares it. He gets 196. Then he takes the square root of 196. What number does he end with?

choices.t: 14 — the square root undoes the square
choices.why: Right! 14² = 196 and √{196} = 14. He is back where he started.

choices.t: 98 — a square root cuts a number in half
choices.why: Half of 196 is 98. A square root asks what number times itself is 196.

choices.t: 196 — a square root does not change it
choices.why: The square root does change 196: √{196} = 14.

choices.t: 38,416 — the square root squares it again
choices.why: 38,416 is 196². Square rooting goes backward, not forward.

hint: What number times itself makes 196?
explain: Kai's number squared is 196. Since 14 × 14 = 196, he started with 14.
He's back to his starting number. Squaring and square rooting are inverse operations: one undoes the other.

stem: Which square root is irrational?

choices.why: Right! 40 is not a perfect square, so √{40} = 6.324… never ends or repeats.
169 is a perfect square: 13 × 13 = 169. So √{169} = 13 is rational.
1 is a perfect square: 1 × 1 = 1. So √{1} = 1 is rational.
121 is a perfect square: 11 × 11 = 121. So √{121} = 11 is rational.

hint: Which number under the root sign is NOT a perfect square?
explain: Their square roots are whole numbers, so they are rational.
40 is between 36 = 6² and 49 = 7², so it is not a perfect square.

x² = 121
x³ = −27

choices.why: 18 × 18 = 324. The square root of 361 is 19.

stem: A cube-shaped water tank holds 27,000 cubic inches. What is the area of one face of the tank?

choices.why: Right! The edge is ∛27,000 = 30 in, and 30² = 900 in².
30 in is the edge length. One face is a 30-by-30 square, so square it.
You divided 27,000 by 3. Take the cube root to find the edge.
You divided 27,000 by 6 faces. Volume is edge³, so take the cube root first.

hint: Volume of a cube = edge³. Find the edge first.
explain: One face is a square: area = 30² = 900 in².

stem: Look at the whole numbers from 20 to 30 (include 20 and 30). How many of them have an irrational square root?

choices.why: Right! Only 25 is a perfect square, so the other 10 have irrational roots.
25 is a perfect square: √{25} = 5, which is rational. Leave it out.
Count again: 20 to 30 is 11 numbers. Take away only 25.
1 is how many are perfect squares. The question asks about irrational roots.

hint: Which perfect squares are between 20 and 30?
explain: Only 25 is in the range 20–30. √{25} = 5 is rational.
The square root of a non-perfect square is irrational, so 10 have irrational roots.

explain: The hundredths digit is 1, so round down: √{58} ≈ 7.6.

stem: Rosa used the estimation algorithm and got √{33} ≈ 5 + {{8|11}} ≈ 5.7. Which argument best proves that √{33} rounds to 5.7?

choices.t: 5.7² = 32.49 and 5.75² ≈ 33.06. 33 is between them, so it rounds to 5.7.
choices.why: Right! √{33} is between 5.7 and 5.75, so it rounds to 5.7.

choices.t: 5.7² = 32.49, which is less than 33. So √{33} rounds to 5.7.
choices.why: This only shows √{33} > 5.7. It could still be 5.8 or 5.9. Check the upper side too.

choices.t: 33 − 25 = 8, so √{33} is 5 and 8 tenths. So it rounds to 5.8.
choices.why: 8 is out of 11 steps, not 10. {{8|11}} ≈ 0.73, so the estimate is about 5.7.

choices.t: 33 is closer to 36 than to 25. So √{33} is about 5.9.
choices.why: Closer to 6 is true, but 5.9² = 34.81 is more than 33. Square to check.
